title: Error Basics & the error Interface
summary: In Go, errors are ordinary values. The built-in `error` is an interface with one method, `Error() string`. Functions return an `error` as their last result, and callers check `if err != nil`. This explicit, value-based approach replaces exceptions and makes failure handling visible in the code.

subtopics.title: The error interface
subtopics.explanation: error is a built-in interface with a single method: Error() string. Any type that implements that method is an error. The zero value of an error is nil, which conventionally means 'no error'. This tiny interface is the whole basis of Go's value-based error handling.

subtopics.title: Returning and checking errors
subtopics.explanation: Idiomatic Go returns (result, error) and the caller immediately checks if err != nil. Errors are handled where they occur, not caught far away. Return early on error to keep the happy path unindented. This return-and-check pattern is how the error interface shows up in everyday code.

subtopics.title: Creating errors
subtopics.explanation: errors.New("msg") makes a simple error. fmt.Errorf("...: %v", x) formats one with context. Use fmt.Errorf with the %w verb to WRAP another error so it can be unwrapped later. These constructors are how you produce the error values the rest of the model relies on.

subtopics.title: Wrapping and unwrapping
subtopics.explanation: Wrapping with %w preserves the original error inside a new one, adding context as it travels up the stack. errors.Is checks whether any error in the chain matches a sentinel; errors.As extracts a specific error type from the chain. This is what lets errors carry context up the stack while callers still recognize the underlying cause.

subtopics.title: Sentinel vs custom errors
subtopics.explanation: A sentinel error is a predeclared value (var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")) compared with errors.Is. A custom error is a struct implementing Error() that can carry fields (codes, fields) and be matched with errors.As. Choosing between them is a core design decision within Go's error interface model.

foundations.overview: Go does not use exceptions for ordinary failures. Instead, errors are plain values: a function that can fail returns an error as its last return value, and the caller checks it explicitly. The error type is just an interface with one method, Error() string. This design makes every failure path visible in the source, trading a little verbosity for a lot of clarity about what can go wrong.
foundations.formalDefinition: error is a built-in interface declaring a single method, Error() string. A nil error conventionally signals success; a non-nil error describes a failure and may wrap an underlying error.
foundations.whyItMatters: Error handling is most of real-world code. Go's explicit, value-based model — plus wrapping with %w and inspection with errors.Is/As — is central to writing robust services and is heavily probed in interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of every fallible call as handing back two things: the result and a note that says 'all good' (nil) or 'here's what went wrong.' You read the note before trusting the result, and you can staple extra context to the note as it's passed upward.
commonUseCases: Wrapping with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) to add context
Detecting specific errors with errors.Is / errors.As
Defining sentinel errors for known conditions

commonMisconceptions.reality: Ordinary failures are returned as error values and checked with if err != nil; panic/recover is reserved for truly exceptional, programmer-level faults.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can compare wrapped errors with ==.
commonMisconceptions.reality: == only matches the exact value. Use errors.Is to match through a wrap chain and errors.As to extract a concrete type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Ignoring an error is fine if it 'usually works'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unchecked errors hide failures; handle, wrap, or explicitly decide to ignore (with a comment) every error.

visualExplorer.title: How an error travels up the stack with wrapping
visualExplorer.caption: Each layer adds context with %w, building a chain that errors.Is/As can inspect.

config.intro: A 'record not found' error bubbling up three layers:

steps.name: Origin
steps.detail: The database layer returns sql.ErrNoRows — a sentinel error meaning the query found nothing.

steps.name: Repository wraps it
steps.detail: repo returns fmt.Errorf("get user %d: %w", id, err), adding context but keeping the original via %w.

steps.name: Service wraps again
steps.detail: The service adds fmt.Errorf("load profile: %w", err); the chain now has three links.

steps.name: Handler inspects the chain
steps.detail: errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) returns true by walking the chain, so the handler maps it to HTTP 404.

steps.name: Log the full context
steps.detail: Logging err prints 'load profile: get user 7: sql: no rows in result set' — the whole story.

interactiveExamples.title: Return and check an error
interactiveExamples.explanation: A fallible function returns (result, error). The caller checks err first and returns early; only then is the result trustworthy.

code.expectedOutput:
ok: 5
error: n is not even

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: wrap the error and detect it with errors.Is
interactiveExamples.explanation: Wrap the underlying error with %w so the caller can still recognize the sentinel ErrNotFound via errors.Is. Edit lookup to wrap, then run the check.

checkpoints.explanation: The zero value of an interface, including error, is nil. So a freshly declared error variable is nil, and err == nil is true — conventionally meaning 'no error'.

checkpoints.prompt: Which method must a type implement to satisfy the built-in `error` interface?
checkpoints.explanation: error is defined as interface { Error() string }. A type satisfies it by implementing Error() string. Unwrap() is optional (for wrapping), and String() is for fmt.Stringer, not error.

checkpoints.prompt: Why won't this reliably detect a wrapped 'not found' error?
options: You can't return a status code
== only matches the exact error, not a wrapped one; use errors.Is
checkpoints.explanation: Because the error is wrapped with %w, err is a new value, not ErrNotFound itself, so == is false. Use errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound), which walks the wrap chain to find a match.

checkpoints.prompt: Wrap err with context while preserving it for errors.Is.
checkpoints.explanation: %w wraps the error, keeping it in the chain so errors.Is/As can find it. %v and %s only format the message text and break the chain; %d is for integers.

codeLab.title: Return an error instead of panicking
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Divide(a, b int) (int, error)` that returns a/b, but returns a wrapped error if b is zero. Define a sentinel `ErrDivideByZero` and wrap it with context so callers can match it with errors.Is.
hints: Check b == 0 first and return early with the error.
Use fmt.Errorf with %w so errors.Is(err, ErrDivideByZero) works.
On success, return the quotient and nil for the error.

debuggingLab.title: Using a result before checking the error
debuggingLab.symptom: On bad input the program prints 0 silently instead of reporting the problem.

brokenCode.code:
n, _ := strconv.Atoi("abc") // error discarded
fmt.Println(n * 2)            // prints 0

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: strconv.Atoi("abc") fails and returns (0, error). By discarding the error with _, the code trusts the zero result and silently computes 0. The failure is invisible — exactly the bug Go's explicit errors are meant to prevent.
commonMistakes: Discarding the error with _ and using the (zero) result anyway.
Assuming a function 'can't really fail' on the inputs you expect.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Check the error and handle it before using the result.

solution.expectedOutput: parse error: strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax

theory.question: How does Go handle errors, and what is the error interface?
theory.directAnswer: Go treats errors as values rather than exceptions. error is a built-in interface with one method, Error() string. Fallible functions return an error as their last result, and callers check if err != nil. A nil error means success. panic/recover exists but is reserved for truly exceptional, unrecoverable situations.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A value-based error model built on a one-method interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make every failure path explicit and visible at the call site instead of hidden in exception control flow.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Functions return (result, error); callers branch on err; errors can be wrapped to add context and inspected with errors.Is/As.

theory.whyImportant: It is the core of idiomatic Go and contrasts sharply with exception-based languages — a guaranteed interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: os.Open returns (*File, error); you check err before using the file handle.

followUps.question: When is panic appropriate instead of returning an error?
followUps.answer: For programmer errors or truly unrecoverable states (e.g., impossible invariants), not for expected failures like bad input or missing files.

followUps.question: What does a nil error signify?
followUps.answer: Success — no error occurred — by universal Go convention.

theory.question: What is error wrapping, and how do errors.Is and errors.As differ?
theory.directAnswer: Wrapping adds context to an error while preserving the original, using fmt.Errorf with the %w verb, forming a chain. errors.Is walks that chain to test whether any error matches a target sentinel value; errors.As walks it to find an error of a particular concrete type and assign it to a variable so you can read its fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A mechanism to enrich errors with context without losing the underlying cause.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So callers can add 'where/what' context as errors travel up, while still detecting the root cause.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: %w stores the wrapped error behind an Unwrap() method; Is compares values down the chain, As type-asserts down the chain.

theory.whyImportant: Correctly wrapping and inspecting errors is essential for good diagnostics and is a frequent senior-level probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler does errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) to return 404, or errors.As(err, &valErr) to read a validation error's Field.

followUps.question: What happens if you use %v instead of %w?
followUps.answer: The original error's text is copied but the chain is broken, so errors.Is/As can no longer find the wrapped error.

followUps.question: Can an error wrap multiple errors?
followUps.answer: Yes — since Go 1.20, errors.Join and fmt.Errorf with multiple %w verbs create errors that wrap several errors at once.

theory.question: What is the difference between a sentinel error and a custom error type, and when would you choose each?
theory.directAnswer: A sentinel error is a single predeclared value, e.g. var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found"), that callers compare against with errors.Is. A custom error is a struct (or other type) that implements Error() string and can carry extra fields like a code or field name; callers extract it with errors.As. Use a sentinel when callers only need to recognize which condition occurred, and a custom type when they need structured data to act on.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to model known error conditions so callers can branch on them.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Callers often need to react differently to specific failures, so errors must be identifiable, not just printable strings.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sentinels are matched by identity through the wrap chain with errors.Is; custom types are matched by dynamic type with errors.As, which also binds a variable so you can read the fields.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right representation shapes a package's public error contract and is a common design question in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: sql.ErrNoRows is a sentinel checked with errors.Is; a *json.SyntaxError is a custom type extracted with errors.As to read its Offset field.

followUps.question: Why should a package export its sentinel errors?
followUps.answer: So callers in other packages can reference the same value with errors.Is; an unexported sentinel can only be matched from within the defining package.

followUps.question: Can a type be both a sentinel-like value and carry data?
followUps.answer: A single custom-error value can be exported as a sentinel and still carry fields, but if callers mutate shared state it becomes unsafe, so prefer immutable values or fresh instances.

theory.question: When should you use panic/recover instead of returning an error, and what are the pitfalls?
theory.directAnswer: Return an error for expected, recoverable failures like bad input, missing files, or network timeouts — that is the vast majority of cases. Reserve panic for truly exceptional, programmer-level faults such as violated invariants or unrecoverable initialization failures. recover is used sparingly, typically at a boundary (like a server request handler) to stop a single panic from crashing the whole process. The main pitfall is using panic as general control flow, which hides failure paths and makes code hard to reason about.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A distinction between value-based error handling and the panic/recover mechanism for exceptional faults.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go separates ordinary, expected failures (visible in signatures) from catastrophic, unexpected faults so control flow stays explicit.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: panic unwinds the stack running deferred functions; a deferred call to recover in the same goroutine stops the unwind and returns the panic value, letting the boundary convert it back into an error.

theory.whyImportant: Misusing panic for normal errors is a classic anti-pattern reviewers and interviewers probe for.
theory.realWorldExample: An HTTP middleware defers recover() so one handler's panic returns 500 for that request instead of taking down the server.

followUps.question: Does recover work across goroutines?
followUps.answer: No — recover only catches a panic in the same goroutine and stack that deferred it; a panic in another goroutine that is not recovered there crashes the program.

followUps.question: Should a library panic on invalid arguments?
followUps.answer: Usually no; return an error so callers can handle it. Panicking is acceptable only for clear programming bugs, like a nil required dependency at construction time.

scenario.question: Your logs show a generic 'operation failed' with no clue where it originated, making incidents slow to debug. How do you improve error reporting?
scenario.directAnswer: The errors lack context. Wrap each error with fmt.Errorf("<operation>: %w", err) as it propagates so the final message reads like a breadcrumb trail, keep sentinel errors for conditions callers must branch on, and log the full wrapped error at the top level. Avoid re-wrapping with the same message and don't both log and return the same error.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A diagnosability problem caused by context-free errors.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Returning bare errors.New strings or using %v loses the origin and the chain.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Adding %w-wrapped context at each layer builds a readable causal chain that errors.Is/As can still inspect.

scenario.whyImportant: Good error context directly shortens incident resolution time.
scenario.realWorldExample: Turning 'operation failed' into 'charge order 42: call payment gateway: connection refused' pinpoints the failure instantly.

followUps.question: Why avoid logging and returning the same error?
followUps.answer: It causes duplicate, noisy log lines; decide on one owner (usually the top of the stack) to log, while lower layers wrap and return.

scenario.question: A refactor replaced fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) with fmt.Errorf("...: %v", err) in a repository layer, and now the HTTP handler that mapped sql.ErrNoRows to a 404 returns 500 for missing records. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Switching %w to %v broke the error chain: %v only copies the underlying error's text into a new string-based error, so errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) no longer finds the sentinel and the handler falls through to its generic 500 case. The fix is to restore %w so the original error stays wrapped and unwrappable. Add a test that asserts errors.Is on the wrapped result to prevent regressions.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A regression caused by breaking the unwrap chain during error formatting.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: %v and %w look almost identical but differ semantically: only %w records the wrapped error behind Unwrap().
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With %w the returned error implements Unwrap(), so errors.Is walks down to sql.ErrNoRows; with %v there is nothing to unwrap, so the walk stops and the match fails.

scenario.whyImportant: This exact mistake silently degrades error handling in production and is a favorite scenario question.
scenario.realWorldExample: After restoring %w, errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) returns true again and the handler correctly maps missing users to HTTP 404.

followUps.question: How would you catch this class of bug automatically?
followUps.answer: Write unit tests asserting errors.Is/errors.As on wrapped results, and consider a linter like errorlint that flags non-wrapping verbs on errors.

systemDesign.question: Design an error-handling strategy for a layered Go service (handler -> service -> repository) so that the API returns correct status codes, logs are diagnosable, and internal details never leak to clients.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define exported sentinel errors (e.g., ErrNotFound, ErrConflict) or custom typed errors in the domain layer. Each lower layer wraps errors with fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) as they propagate, never logging in the middle. The HTTP handler is the single boundary that inspects with errors.Is/errors.As to choose a status code, logs the full wrapped error once for internal diagnostics, and returns a sanitized, generic message to the client. This keeps the causal chain intact for operators while hiding internals from users.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cross-cutting design that maps internal errors to a stable external contract.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Layers have different concerns: repositories know causes, handlers know how to present them, and clients must not see stack details or SQL text.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrapping preserves the chain upward; the boundary uses errors.Is/As to classify, logs once at the top, and translates to a status code plus a safe message. Sentinels/typed errors form the vocabulary the boundary switches on.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Consistent error mapping is essential for reliable APIs and observable systems, and layered design questions are common in interviews.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A repo returns sql.ErrNoRows; the service wraps it as 'load profile: %w'; the handler does errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows), logs the full chain, and responds 404 with {"error":"resource not found"}.

followUps.question: Where should errors be logged in this design?
followUps.answer: Once, at the boundary (the handler) that has full context and decides the response; lower layers only wrap and return to avoid duplicate log lines.

followUps.question: How do you avoid leaking internal details to clients?
followUps.answer: Map internal errors to a small set of safe, generic messages and status codes at the boundary, and never render the wrapped error string in the response body.

coding.question: Implement a custom error type `ValidationError` with a Field and Message, and a function `Validate(name string) error` that returns it (wrapped) when name is empty. Show how a caller extracts it with errors.As.
coding.thoughtProcess: Define a struct with the fields, implement Error() string to satisfy the interface, and return a pointer to it. Use a pointer receiver and pointer value so errors.As can match *ValidationError. Wrap it for context, then in the caller use errors.As to pull the concrete type out and read Field.
coding.lineByLine: ValidationError carries structured data and implements Error() with a pointer receiver, so *ValidationError is an error. Validate returns it wrapped with %w for context. In handle, errors.As walks the chain and, on a match, sets ve to the underlying *ValidationError, letting us read ve.Field — something a plain string error couldn't provide.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) where d is the wrap-chain depth (tiny in practice).

followUps.question: Why use a pointer receiver and &ValidationError{}?
followUps.answer: errors.As matches on the dynamic type; using *ValidationError consistently ensures the target var *ValidationError matches.

followUps.question: When prefer a sentinel error over a custom type?
followUps.answer: Use a sentinel when callers only need to know 'which condition'; use a custom type when they need extra data (field name, code, retryability).

coding.question: Implement ProcessAll(items []string, fn func(string) error) error that runs fn on every item, collects all failures, and returns a single error combining them (using errors.Join) or nil if none failed. Show how a caller checks whether a specific sentinel occurred.
coding.thoughtProcess: Rather than stopping at the first failure, accumulate errors so the caller sees every problem. Collect each non-nil error into a slice, then combine with errors.Join, which returns nil if the slice is empty and otherwise an error that wraps all of them. Because errors.Join preserves each wrapped error, errors.Is still works against the combined value to detect a specific sentinel.
coding.lineByLine: ProcessAll iterates items and calls fn on each; a non-nil result is wrapped with context via %w and appended to errs. errors.Join(errs...) returns nil when errs is empty and otherwise a combined error whose Unwrap() []error exposes every wrapped error. In main, check returns the ErrEmpty sentinel for blank strings; the combined error is non-nil, and errors.Is(err, ErrEmpty) returns true because Join keeps each wrapped error matchable.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the items, plus O(k) to join k failures.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the k collected errors.

followUps.question: How does errors.Is work against an errors.Join result?
followUps.answer: The joined error implements Unwrap() []error, so errors.Is checks each contained error (and its chain), returning true if any matches the target.

followUps.question: When would you stop at the first error instead of joining?
followUps.answer: When failures are dependent or expensive to continue past — for example, if a later step needs an earlier step's output, return early instead of accumulating.

keyTakeaways: Errors are values: error is an interface with one method, Error() string, and nil means success.
Fallible functions return (result, error); check if err != nil and return early before trusting the result.
Wrap with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) to add context while preserving the cause; use errors.Is/errors.As to inspect the chain.
Reserve panic/recover for truly exceptional faults — ordinary failures are handled explicitly as returned errors.
